name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,362

entries.clue: Dog barking around European city (9)

indicatorNotes.around: To turn a thing around is to set it facing the other way, so the word just named is written back to front.

blocks.note: a rotter is a thoroughgoing cad, the same insult carried by calling a man a dirty dog
barking on its own means mad, and the turn sends those three letters the other way

annotation.surface: A dog yapping its way round a city somewhere in Europe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like the noise the dog is making and means mad, the way British speech shortens 'barking mad'. Nothing in the clue points at the Netherlands.
annotation.definitionFit: Rotterdam is the great Dutch port at the mouth of the Rhine, so the definition names it by its class rather than describing it.

entries.clue: Affluent church supporting religion in schools (4)

indicatorNotes.supporting: A support stands underneath what it holds up, so in a down clue the church goes at the foot, below the letters named after it.

blocks.note: RI is religious instruction, the name British school timetables give the subject
CH is the standard short form of church, as printed on a map

annotation.surface: Well-off parishioners backing the teaching of religion in the classroom.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue writes the church first and the grid wants it last, which is the whole job 'supporting' is doing. RI is what a British school report calls the religion lesson.
annotation.definitionFit: Rich means having plenty of money, which is what affluent says in a longer word.

entries.clue: Thief in East London, one of the dregs? (3,4)

blocks.note: East London is Cockney country, and Cockney rhyming slang swaps a word for a short phrase ending on a rhyme for it
the sodden scraps left in the bottom of the pot once it has been poured out

annotation.surface: A pickpocket from the East End written off as the lowest of the low.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the second reading as a joke rather than a dictionary sense: the dregs are the rubbish of society in the surface and the sediment in the pot in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang, spoken in East London, makes tea leaf a thief; read straight it is also the sediment left at the bottom of the pot.

entries.clue: Amount of work Etonian recruit gets initially (3)

indicatorNotes.initially: What happens initially happens at the very start, so only the opening letter of each word before it is taken.

blocks.note: the three words give up their first letters in the order they stand

annotation.surface: A new boy at Eton finding out how much work is expected of him.
annotation.walkthrough: Eton is the English public school, so 'Etonian recruit' reads as a new pupil and neither word means anything to the grid beyond the letter it starts with. The definition names a quantity, not a job.
annotation.definitionFit: An erg is the unit of work in the old centimetre-gram-second system, the work done by a force of one dyne moving through one centimetre.

entries.clue: Scientist’s venture largely secure (6)

indicatorNotes.largely: Largely means for the most part and not the whole, so the word beside it arrives one letter short at its end.

blocks.note: to venture is to dare, and it stops before its final letter
to secure a prize or a contract is to win it

annotation.surface: A researcher's gamble paying off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Venture' and 'secure' both read as business words, which is why neither looks like a synonym waiting to be chopped. The surname is the definition's whole content, given only by trade.
annotation.definitionFit: Charles Darwin, the naturalist who published On the Origin of Species in 1859, is named here by his trade rather than by anything he did.

entries.clue: Amusing rogue entertaining English male element (9)

indicatorNotes.rogue: A rogue keeps to no proper order, so the letters standing beside the word will not stay as they are written.
indicatorNotes.entertaining: To entertain guests is to have them in, so the two letters named next join the ones being shuffled.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters
E is the usual single letter for English
m is the standard short form of male

annotation.surface: A likeable scoundrel putting on a show for an Englishman.
annotation.walkthrough: Nine letters wanted from a seven-letter word is the shape that tells you abbreviations are being folded in. 'Rogue' is a noun in the surface and an instruction in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: Magnesium is the light silvery metal that burns with a blinding white flame, number twelve in the periodic table, so 'element' names it by its class.

entries.clue: Policeman’s constant work (3)

blocks.note: c is the physicist's constant, the speed of light
op is opus, the composer's numbered work

annotation.surface: An officer's unending shift.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Constant work' reads as one phrase about a policeman who never gets a break, and the two words belong to different pieces of the charade. Each is a standard abbreviation.
annotation.definitionFit: Cop is the everyday word for a police officer, from 'to cop' meaning to catch.

entries.clue: Vineyard associated with holy man’s livelihood (5)

blocks.note: cru is the French wine word for a named vineyard and the growth it yields, as in grand cru
a holy man canonised by the church is a saint, shortened to St

annotation.surface: A monastery's wine trade keeping the brothers fed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vineyard' has to be taken in French before anything else works, which is the one step a solver without the wine word cannot make. Earning a crust is British for earning a living.
annotation.definitionFit: To earn a crust is British idiom for earning your living, so the bread word stands in for the living itself.

entries.clue: Father joining gym outwardly reveals ID? (6)

annotation.definitionNote: ID is singular and the answer is plural, but a person's ID is routinely a sheaf of documents rather than one, and the question mark marks the definition as a use of the answer rather than a synonym for it.

indicatorNotes.outwardly: Outwardly means at the outside, so only the first and last letters of the word beside it are taken.

blocks.note: pa is the familiar word for father
PE is physical education, the gym lesson on a British school timetable
the outermost letters of REVEALS, its first and its last

annotation.surface: A dad signing up at the gym and having to prove who he is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reveals' looks like the verb the sentence turns on and is a word stripped to its two edges instead. The definition is the two bare letters at the end, which is why the eye slides past them.
annotation.definitionFit: Papers are the documents — passport, licence, permit — a person produces to show who they are, which is what a demand for ID asks for.

entries.clue: Mistake with chlorine leading to irritation (7)

blocks.note: Cl is the chemical symbol for chlorine
irritation in the sense of being annoyed is anger

annotation.surface: A slip with the pool chemicals that leaves everybody's eyes stinging.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface works because chlorine really does irritate, so both words look like chemistry and only the first is doing chemical work. The irritation wanted is the temper, not the rash.
annotation.definitionFit: To drop a clanger is British idiom for making a blunder everybody notices, so the word names a mistake by the noise it makes.

entries.clue: Doctor welcoming odd one with complaint? (5)

indicatorNotes.welcoming: To welcome somebody is to take them inside, so the word named before goes round the one that follows.

blocks.note: a GP is the general practitioner, the family doctor
rum is an old British word for odd or peculiar, as in 'a rum do'

annotation.surface: A doctor cheerfully taking in a patient with a strange ailment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' is the pivot: an illness in the surgery and a grumble in the grid, and the question mark is the only warning. 'One' belongs to the definition rather than supplying a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A grump is somebody forever finding fault, so the definition names the person by the thing they always have to hand.

entries.clue: Cheese Lee redirects wrongly (3,9)

indicatorNotes.wrongly: Done wrongly means not done as it should be, so the letters beside the word come out in an order other than their own.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Somebody called Lee sending the traffic the wrong way.
annotation.walkthrough: A proper name at the head of the fodder makes the whole thing read as news rather than as letters, and the definition is left stranded at the front. Twelve letters is long enough that the crossings usually arrive first.
annotation.definitionFit: Red Leicester is the orange-red English cow's-milk cheese from Leicestershire, milder and more crumbly than cheddar.

entries.clue: Oscar succeeded getting through Tolkien novel having tenuous connections (5,4)

indicatorNotes.novel: Novel means new and unfamiliar, so the name beside it is set out in an arrangement that is not its own.
indicatorNotes.getting through: To get through a thing is to make your way inside it, so the two letters named first land within the letters that follow.

blocks.note: the seven letters of the author's name in another order
O is Oscar in the radio alphabet
s is the standard short form of succeeded

annotation.surface: A man called Oscar finally reaching the end of a long fantasy novel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tolkien novel' looks like a title waiting to be supplied — The Hobbit, The Silmarillion — and it is the author's own name being shuffled instead. 'Novel' does the shuffling from inside that phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: Something loose-knit is held together only slackly, its parts barely joined, which is what having tenuous connections amounts to.

entries.clue: Hairstyle reflected in mirror fabulous (4)

indicatorNotes.reflected: What a mirror reflects comes back the other way about, so the buried letters are read from right to left.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' says the letters are to be found inside the words that follow, running unbroken across the gap between them.

blocks.note: a run of four letters straddling the gap between the two words, taken from right to left

annotation.surface: A hairdo that looks wonderful in the glass.
annotation.walkthrough: The turn and the hiding place are packed into the two ordinary words 'reflected in', which is what makes the span so hard to see. A short hidden answer is worth checking backwards as well as forwards.
annotation.definitionFit: An afro is the rounded mass of tightly curled hair worn out from the head, the style named for where it came from.

entries.clue: Long throw lacking power (4)

indicatorNotes.lacking: What a thing lacks it has not got, so the letter named after the word is struck out of it.

blocks.note: to throw a ball is to pitch it
p is the physicist's short form for power, and it is the letter taken away

annotation.surface: A throw that does not carry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long' opens the clue looking like an adjective about the throw and is the verb meaning to yearn. The letter comes off the front, which is where a deletion is hardest to spot.
annotation.definitionFit: To itch for something is to want it restlessly, which is what to long for it means.

entries.clue: I’m leaving food generally, current and old (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a sentence rather than a synonym, because the answer is not a word about departure but the word a departing person says; the clue defines it by what saying it announces.

blocks.note: cheer is the old word for fare — food in general, as in a table of good cheer
I is the physicist's symbol for electric current
o is the dictionary's short form for old

annotation.surface: Somebody walking out and leaving the food behind, this year's and last.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cheer' for food is the oldest word in the clue: the good cheer of a Christmas table is a spread, not a mood. 'Current and old' pairs two abbreviations that look like a contrast.
annotation.definitionFit: Cheerio is the British goodbye, the word said by the one doing the leaving, so the definition quotes what saying it announces.

entries.clue: Strongly affect this writer’s agreement (6)

blocks.note: the setter speaking of himself is I, and 'this writer is' contracts to those two letters
an agreement struck between two parties is a pact

annotation.surface: The deal the author of the piece has signed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter's standard way of putting himself into a clue, and the apostrophe-s belongs to the letters, not to a possessive waiting for its noun.
annotation.definitionFit: To impact something is to affect it with force, the verb having moved from physical collision to any strong effect.

entries.clue: Daughter, six, overwhelmed by excellent guidance (6)

indicatorNotes.overwhelmed by: To be overwhelmed by something is to be covered over by it, so the letters named first are written inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: ace means excellent, first-rate
d is the family-tree short form of daughter
VI is six in Roman numerals

annotation.surface: A six-year-old daughter swamped by first-rate guidance.
annotation.walkthrough: The commas make 'Daughter, six' read as a child and her age, and they are two separate abbreviations. 'Overwhelmed by' is the only thing saying which piece goes outside.
annotation.definitionFit: Advice is what one person tells another they ought to do, which is guidance given in words.

entries.clue: Manage what a joiner might do (4,4,4)

blocks.note: to get by on the money coming in, with nothing to spare
a joiner is the carpenter who fits woodwork together, and bringing two ends up against each other is the job

annotation.surface: Getting by, the way a carpenter does.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition takes the idiom literally, which is the joke: a joiner really does bring two ends together. 'Might' marks it as one of the things a joiner does rather than the whole trade.
annotation.definitionFit: To make ends meet is to stretch the income to cover the outgoings, which is managing; word by word it is also what a joiner does at the bench.

entries.clue: King with northern individual widely recognised (5)

blocks.note: K is the chess and card short form for king
n is the compass short form for northern
your own way is the individual one, belonging to you alone

annotation.surface: A monarch from the north who is very much his own man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Northern individual' reads as one person from one place and splits into a single letter and a word. The adjective sense of 'individual' is the one wanted, not the noun the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: Something known is recognised by everyone likely to come across it, so 'widely recognised' is that adjective in longer words.

entries.clue: Staff voting in auditorium (4)

indicatorNotes.in auditorium: An auditorium is a place built for hearing, so the word is to be taken by its sound rather than by its spelling.

blocks.note: a vote taken is a poll, and that sound is written down here another way

annotation.surface: An election held in a concert hall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Voting in' is exactly how a result gets reported, so the sound marker hides inside a natural phrase. The two spellings differ by one letter and sound identical.
annotation.definitionFit: A pole is a long rounded shaft of wood, which is what a staff is when someone leans on it or plants a flag on it.

entries.clue: Katrina regularly protecting party dress (5)

indicatorNotes.regularly: Letters taken regularly come at a fixed interval, and the interval here is every other letter, counting from the second.
indicatorNotes.protecting: What protects a thing is wrapped round it, so the letters named before close over the word that follows.

blocks.note: every second letter of the name, counting from the second
a do is a party, the British word for an occasion with drinks

annotation.surface: A woman called Katrina forever looking after somebody's party frock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Party dress' reads as one garment and splits in two: the first word is wordplay and the second is the definition. Only the even letters of the name are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: To adorn something is to dress it up with ornament, the sense 'dress' carries when a table or a shop window is dressed.

entries.clue: Minor, uncovered, admitting plant fire (7)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: A thing uncovered has lost what lay over it at either end, so the word gives up its first and last letters.
indicatorNotes.admitting: To admit somebody is to let them in, so the letters left go round the word that follows.

blocks.note: MINOR with the letter at each end taken off
a fern is the shade-loving plant with fronds and no flowers

annotation.surface: A youngster found out and owning up to the blaze at the factory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant' is a factory in the surface and something green in the grid. 'Admitting' is a confession in one reading and an instruction to let letters inside in the other.
annotation.definitionFit: An inferno is a fire raging out of control, the word borrowed from Dante's hell.

entries.clue: Enemy of revolutionary European (3)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: A revolution turns a thing right round, so the word before it is written the other way about.

blocks.note: the two letters of OF turned back to front
E is the standard single letter for European

annotation.surface: The natural enemy of a European radical.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enemy of' reads as one phrase and the 'of' is wordplay, which is the whole trick in a three-letter clue. 'Revolutionary' is a person in the surface and a turn in the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A foe is one who is set against you, the older and shorter word for an enemy.

entries.clue: Weight not to be returned (3)

indicatorNotes.returned: What is returned comes back the way it went, so the word before it is read from its end to its start.

blocks.note: the three letters of NOT read from the back

annotation.surface: A consignment nobody is allowed to send back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not to be returned' reads as one instruction stamped on a label; the grid takes 'not' as the word and the rest as the order to turn it. Three-letter reversals are usually the last thing a solver checks.
annotation.definitionFit: A ton is the standard large unit of weight, 2,240 pounds in Britain, so the definition names it by what it measures.

entries.clue: For that reason, the group of soldiers watch out (9)

blocks.note: the article taken as itself
RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army corps that builds the bridges and clears the mines
the warning a golfer shouts before the ball reaches anybody

annotation.surface: Telling the sappers to keep their eyes open.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Watch out' is a shouted warning in both readings, and only on a golf course is it a single four-letter word. RE is the corps a setter reaches for whenever soldiers are wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: Therefore introduces the conclusion that follows from what has just been said, which is what 'for that reason' does in plainer words.
